_podcast.theme_scoring_prompt:
Rate how well this article fits the theme 'Arts, Culture & Digital Storytelling' — how communities create, preserve, and share culture, with particular interest in the Cariboo and rural BC.

OUT OF SCOPE — score 0-14: medical and health research with no cultural angle; resource-economy stories with no cultural framing; wildlife and nature stories without a creative or community-media context; data centre and AI investment news; geopolitical conflict, war, and crime coverage; financial market stories.

CALIBRATION — apply this ladder to everything else. A Cariboo tie raises a score but is NOT required to reach the top band: judge on the strength of the arts/culture/storytelling reporting first.
- 80-100: Excellent arts, culture, or storytelling journalism. Cariboo/Williams Lake arts news lands here (arts council grants, murals, local festivals, Indigenous film, community theatre, heritage programs, a Cariboo author or artist honoured) — and so does outstanding national or international cultural reporting with real depth.
- 55-79: Solid arts/culture/media journalism. Rural BC and Canadian cultural coverage, CBC Arts features, regional festivals, community media projects, heritage preservation, creative-economy stories, digital storytelling tools and platforms, community media tech (podcasting, streaming, local publishing), animation and film production. Most genuine cultural journalism belongs HERE, not below.
- 30-54: Mainstream entertainment-industry coverage with modest substance (awards-show results, film/TV/music business news, publishing trade news).
- 15-29: Tangentially creative — a tech feature touching media/publishing/streaming, or Cariboo civic news with no arts angle.

ANCHORS: 'Repatriated Tŝilhqot'in baskets arrive in Williams Lake from Brooklyn Museum' → 95. 'How a BC First Nation is digitizing its oral histories' → 80. 'CBC Arts: the quiet revival of small-town prairie theatre' → 68. 'Netflix reports Q3 subscriber growth' → 20.

Score 0-100 where 100 is a perfect thematic match and 0 is completely unrelated.

items.title: [Nieman Storyboard] Personal stories of 9/11, 25 years later
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Sign up for the Nieman Storyboard newsletter, delivered every Friday in your inbox.

***

Dear Storyboard community:

I moved from California to New York City in late August 2001. 

I had been living in Manhattan for two weeks when I showed up for work in Times Square and discovered that a plane had struck the North Tower of the World Trade Center, just a few miles south. 

After the second plane struck the South Tower at 9:03 am ET, our office building was evacuated. I gathered my belongings, walked east to Fifth Avenue, and slowly made my way uptown, turning around every couple blocks to see the massive plumes of smoke in the distance. 

By the time I reached Central Park, crowds gathered around televisions outside the CBS News studios on 59th Street. I remember the looks on people's faces, in tears, in shock, as they replayed footage of the South Tower collapsing. 

In the days that followed, I spent many nights in Union Square, on 14th Street. It had become a gathering place for candlelight vigils and collective grieving. Posters for missing friends and family members were taped up everywhere. 

I felt fortunate to be a part of this community as it came together, to be a witness to it. But for many years I felt like this was not my story to tell. I lost no friends or family members. I was barely even a New Yorker. What right did I have to share my experience? 

And yet, as I've gotten older I've come to appreciate the importance of telling my own stories. My daughters have interviewed me about 9/11 for school reports. As Garrett Graff writes for National Geographic, “Today some 40 percent of the country is too young to remember the events of 9/11.” Every story, however small, adds to our collective memory and shared understanding. They connect us. 

I think frequently about the power of "Portraits of Grief,” the New York Times project in which reporters crafted 200-word vignettes for 2,310 of the nearly 3,000 people who died on 9/11. “We weren't mourning an anonymous mass of people, we were mourning thousands of individuals,” the late novelist Paul Auster wrote about the profiles in 2001. “And the more we knew about them, the more we could wrestle with our own grief.”

For more stories and remembrances from 9/11, see the Nieman Storyboard archive.

You have your own story to share, too. My guest on this week's Nieman Storyboard podcast, author and editor Sari Botton, taught me so much about the power of personal storytelling when she was the essays editor for Longreads. She's now editor and publisher of popular Substack publications including Oldster Magazine and Memoir Land, and she's written her own memoir, “And You May Find Yourself…Confessions of a Late-Blooming Gen-X Weirdo.” She shares some important insights about her journey, as well as advice for writers who might be working on their own personal stories.

Author and editor Sari Botton on giving yourself permission to write personal essays

“People are so concerned about whether they're going to be a likable character if they tell the ugly truth. [But] that's what makes you a likable character. It makes you someone that people can relate to. It means you're just human.”

[ Read the story ]


[ Follow us in Apple Podcasts, Spotify, or your favorite podcast app. ]

Links of note

  • “Don’t Make My Mistakes: A Guide to Reporting in Unfamiliar Places.” For Study Hall, journalist Hannah Docter-Loeb breaks down the key questions reporters should consider when writing about a community that is new to them. 

  • Science journalist Christian Elliott explains how one of his sources for a National Geographic story, a 77-year-old retired librarian named Phil Gordon, was so interesting that he became the main character in an entirely different profile. “I spent maybe two hours with Gordon in total,” Elliott writes. “In that time, he dropped so many quotable lines I had more material than I knew what to do with. When we drove up (and parked behind his dented white pickup, full of driftwood logs collected on the beach for unspecified reasons), [we] found him sitting on a rickety wooden platform dangling over Pacific Ocean. He offered us bourbon and peanut butter.”

  • Journalist Leah Sottile reflects on six years of writing her newsletter (and perhaps another data point in whether you should start your own): “It has since become a major part of my writing life — a thing I very much look forward to working on each month. So, yeah, I guess it made me feel better. Sometimes the writing comes to me easily, sometimes I totally panic about writing something worthy of your hard-earned dollars. It has never been my goal to be the biggest writer on Substack, and it shocks me every time I meet someone in the real world who says they are one of the 5,132 people reading this newsletter every month. There is something that just punches me in the heart every time I hear that, makes me feel so seen, like I’m not just out here making my hands arthritic for no good reason.” 

Keep writing and sharing your stories,

Mark Armstrong
Editor
Nieman Storyboard
Follow the Nieman Storyboard Podcast 
On Bluesky: @niemanstoryboard.org

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Scientists find a weak spot in one of the deadliest brain cancers
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Researchers may have found a new way to weaken glioblastoma’s defenses against treatment. Blocking a protein called SET prevented tumors from forming in preclinical models, while targeting related proteins made cancer cells more vulnerable to radiation. The strategy works by restoring activity of PP2A, an enzyme that glioblastoma cells appear to suppress. Human testing will be needed to determine whether the approach is safe and effective.

items.title: [Fast Company] How ‘Star Trek’ helped invent the future
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Star Trek first beamed into our lives at 8:30 p.m. on Sept. 8, 1966, and the science fiction world was never the same. The show, though canceled after just three seasons, went on to become a lasting pop culture phenomenon that has spawned an entertainment empire, with movies, spinoffs, merchandise, and a fan following that few intellectual properties can match.

But Star Trek proved to be more than just an entertainment property. The technology the show imagined inspired many future developers to try to recreate the gadgets they saw growing up. And some of those fantastical devices have become part of daily life, even if we’re still a long way from launching our own five-year mission to explore strange new worlds.

Here’s some of the on-screen technology that has become real.

Communicators

Captain Kirk and crew stayed in touch with each other and the Enterprise via a handheld device that flipped open. Modern technology managed to replicate that by 1989, with the release of the first Motorola StarTAC phone, and arguably perfected it with the Razr in 2004.

The technology, of course, has continued to improve, and the “communicators” we carry today, in the form of iPhones and the wide assortment of Android devices, do a lot more than just let us talk to others. Still, Martin Cooper, who has been credited with the invention of the first handheld cellular phone in the 1970s, said his inspiration for the first cell phone was, in fact, Star Trek‘s communicator.

Universal translators

Lt. Uhura had lots of duties on board the Enterprise, but figuring out what the aliens were saying wasn’t always one of them. That was the job of the ship’s universal translator. Today, there are several tools that provide instant translation of foreign languages, though they’re not too useful should a Gorn want to strike up a conversation.

Those range from apps such as Google Translate and iTranslate to AI-assisted earbuds like the Samsung Galaxy Buds4 line and Timekettle’s W4 Pro, as well as handheld translators like the Vasco V4 Language Translator Device.

Voice-interface computers

In 1966, seeing Mr. Spock talk with the ship’s computer was something few people could imagine. Today, millions of people do that on a regular basis, interacting with the Amazon Echo device sitting on their counter, asking Siri to call up some information, or even telling their vacuum to tidy up the floors. Most states, in fact, require drivers to avoid picking up their cell phones while behind the wheel but are just fine with voice interactions.

Medical tricorders

Dr. McCoy isn’t the only person with a tricorder medical scanner, though his is still much better than anything we have at the moment. A decade ago, a company called Scanadu showed off a handheld device that measured five vital signs in roughly 30 seconds. That company was acquired six years ago by Israeli healthcare startup Healthy.io.

Today’s smartwatches, meanwhile, fill some of the same roles as a tricorder, monitoring your heart rate, sleep schedule, blood pressure, and more.

Replicators

The advent of 3D printers has given us the ability to summon devices from thin air, much like viewers have seen in subsequent Star Trek shows (though it sometimes takes a day or two for them to assemble). The technology can create everything from custom prosthetics to engine parts to rocket engines, as used on the Aeon 1 rocket in 2023.

3D-printed food as it was presented on the show isn’t possible, but specialized devices can create edible layers using food powders and a liquid binder. That can make a decent confection, but it’s still a long way from learning to make Gagh.

Hyposprays

Shots on Star Trek were needle-free, something any child watching was particularly envious of. What few realized, though, was that jet injectors were actually already a thing at the time. The device uses high-pressure gas to propel a high-velocity stream of liquid medication through the skin. The tech is still around today, but doctors haven’t given up the needle for the most part. Sorry, kids.

(Coming soon?) Warp drive

OK, no, the warp drive is still a fantasy. Faster-than-light travel, as NASA will tell anyone who asks, is still imaginary at present. That doesn’t mean it has given up on the idea. NASA’s Glenn Research Center in Cleveland, Ohio, houses the Breakthrough Propulsion Physics Project, where NASA engineers are hoping to produce “near-term, credible, and measurable progress toward the technology breakthroughs needed to revolutionize space travel and enable interstellar voyages.” The Tau Zero Foundation, meanwhile, is also seeking advances in propulsion that could make interstellar flight possible.
